questions.q: What makes HS256 a symmetric signing algorithm?
o: The same secret both creates and verifies the signature
A public key verifies tokens that a private key signed
The payload is encrypted so only the HS256 holder can read it
Two different HMAC keys are required, one for each direction
questions.x: HS256 is HMAC-SHA256. One shared secret signs the token and verifies it. That differs from RS256, which uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify.
questions.h: Symmetric means one key works both ways. What is shared between signing and verifying?

questions.q: Why can a weak HS256 secret be cracked without talking to the server?
o: The server returns the secret whenever a forged token is rejected
HS256 embeds a copy of the secret inside the encoded payload
The JWT already contains everything needed to test candidate secrets
Each guess must hit the server so it can confirm a matching HMAC
questions.x: The signature is deterministic: same input and same key always produce the same signature. An attacker takes the header and payload, signs them with wordlist secrets, and compares the result to the original signature.
questions.h: HMAC checks need the signed data, the algorithm, and a guessed key. Which of those are already in the captured JWT?

questions.q: When is brute-forcing an HS256 secret actually feasible?
o: Whenever RS256 is used and the public key is published
When the secret is weak and already present in common wordlists
Only when the attacker also has the server private key on disk
Only after the token expires and the signature is no longer checked
questions.x: Offline guessing only works if the secret is weak enough to appear in a wordlist, such as secret, password, or secret1. A long random secret is not practical to brute-force this way.
questions.h: The attack tries secrets from a list. What kind of key will that list actually contain?

questions.q: How does an attacker confirm that a guessed HS256 secret is correct?
o: They decrypt the payload and look for the secret as a claim
They send the guess to /jwks.json and wait for a 200 response
They check whether the alg header changes from HS256 to none
They re-sign the same header and payload and compare signatures
questions.x: Because HMAC is deterministic, a correct guess produces a signature identical to the one on the captured token. A mismatch means that candidate is wrong.
questions.h: Same input plus same key always yields the same HMAC. How do you use that fact to test a guess?

questions.q: Which kind of HS256 secret is most at risk of a wordlist attack?
o: A long random value never copied from documentation
A short common string such as secret or password
A unique 256-bit key stored only in server memory
A public JWKS key used only for RS256 verification
questions.x: HS256 security depends entirely on secret strength. Values like secret, password, or secret1 are in common wordlists, so they can be found by comparing signatures offline.
questions.h: The partial names a few example secrets. What do those examples have in common?
